author: hprotagonist
cardQuote: A VC-backed pip-and-more doesn't make sense to me. It's 2024: what's the revenue model when the free money printer's on the fritz?
quote: A VC-backed pip-and-more doesn't make sense to me. It's 2024: what's the revenue model when the free money printer's on the fritz?
outcome: uv became a near-standard Python package manager, and OpenAI agreed to acquire Astral in March 2026.
outcomeDetail: uv launched in February 2024 as a fast drop-in replacement for pip, then expanded into project management, Python installs, and lockfiles. By 2026 it was widely described as part of the foundation of modern Python development. OpenAI announced it would acquire Astral, the company behind uv, Ruff, and ty.
note: hprotagonist treated a faster pip replacement as a venture-funded vanity project; uv instead became the default in much of the Python ecosystem and ended up inside OpenAI.

author: culi
cardQuote: In the latest StackOverflow survey (2022), Svelte still hasn't even surpassed the 5% threshold for how many developers have used it.
quote: and before angular was jquery. But I do think there's quite a big difference between React and Angular. Angular never reached the level of marketshare that React has even if it was close. And even when it was close it was only for a few years. React has been the standard for nearly a decade now. And React has been much more explicit about growing its ecosystem whereas Angular has much fewer 3rd party plugins/tools. In addition to all that, Svelte has technically been around since 2016. Even if we cheat and say it only really started getting attention in 2018-2020, it has still been rising slower than Vue did when it launched. In the latest StackOverflow survey (2022), Svelte still hasn't even surpassed the 5% threshold for how many developers have used it. By pretty much every metric,[^0] svelte is a tiny community still. A darling of the web dev community for sure, but has not yet gained the confidence of commercial products. Perhaps this has actually been good for Svelte and its development. It definitely seems like it's heading towards much wider adoption so I guess we'll see it tested soon enough [^0]: https://gist.github.com/tkrotoff/b1caa4c3a185629299ec234d231...
outcome: Svelte 5 shipped in 2024, and SvelteKit remained a major full-stack framework used by Hugging Face's Gradio.
outcomeDetail: SvelteKit 1.0 shipped in December 2022, followed by Svelte 5 in October 2024. Hugging Face's Gradio, used by roughly a million developers a month, runs on SvelteKit. The framework remains one of the main non-React full-stack options.
note: culi's survey numbers were accurate at the time, but the conclusion that Svelte was too small for commercial products underestimated how quickly SvelteKit would become a production default.

author: midrus
cardQuote: I think in an SPA, traditional form posts and server redirects are a terrible idea. This might work for q blog post example, but imagine doing a full reload just because you liked a post or a comment.
quote: I think in an SPA, traditional form posts and server redirects are a terrible idea. This might work for q blog post example, but imagine doing a full reload just because you liked a post or a comment.
storyTitle: Remix – A framework focused on web fundamentals and modern UX
outcome: Shopify acquired Remix in October 2022 and made it central to its Hydrogen storefront stack.
outcomeDetail: Remix's core bet was that HTML forms and server-side data loading could be progressively enhanced rather than replaced by client-side fetch. Shopify acquired the company in October 2022 and built Hydrogen on the framework. Remix's loader/action model later shaped React Router's data APIs.
note: midrus assumed Remix would force full page reloads, missing that its entire pitch was intercepting form submissions and enhancing them in the browser. The framework's form model was vindicated by Shopify's acquisition.

author: rvz
cardQuote: It's basically exposing a Rust API and using FFI to the Desktop APIs. Nothing special going on apart from hype and marketing and possible over-promising on features.
quote: > What's the point of mentioning Rust when the heavylifting is done by the system's webview widget, and applications are written in HTML/CSS/JS, just as in Electron? That is true. It's basically exposing a Rust API and using FFI to the Desktop APIs. Nothing special going on apart from hype and marketing and possible over-promising on features. > Isn't the whole point of Electron to have version/feature stability for the browser APIs by bundling a specific Chromium runtime? Yes. The selling point here is that there are no fundamental rewrites needed for using Electron but only small Javascript / Typescript tweaks to get it up and running. This is why unfortunately Electron is used all the time despite the giant negatives. As with Tauri, it is basically a wrapper around the system Webview and using Rust FFI to the Desktop APIs. I'd rather bet on Flutter Desktop as a possible long term Electron competitor.
storyTitle: Tauri 1.0 – Electron Alternative Powered by Rust
outcome: Tauri 2.0 shipped in October 2024 with mobile support, and the project passed 80,000 GitHub stars.
outcomeDetail: Tauri 2.0 arrived in October 2024 with iOS and Android support and a reworked plugin system. The project grew past 80,000 GitHub stars and became the main lightweight alternative to Electron for Rust-based desktop apps.
note: rvz reduced Tauri to a system-webview wrapper and bet on Flutter Desktop instead. Tauri's Rust backend, small binaries, and mobile support turned out to be a durable combination.

author: jaequery
cardQuote: Is this backward compatible with other React packages? Otherwise, I’m afraid it may just turn out to be Yet Another Js Framework.
quote: Is this backward compatible with other React packages? Otherwise, I’m afraid it may just turn out to be Yet Another Js Framework.
outcome: SolidStart 1.0 shipped in 2024, and Solid's signals model was adopted by Angular, Vue, and Svelte.
outcomeDetail: SolidStart 1.0 shipped in May 2024. Solid's fine-grained signals approach was adopted by Angular Signals, Vue Vapor, and Svelte 5's runes, making Solid one of the most influential frontend projects of its generation even without React-scale adoption.
note: The 'Yet Another JS Framework' label missed the substance: Solid's reactivity model became the blueprint for the next generation of Angular, Vue, and Svelte.

storyTitle: Show HN: Codeium – a free, fast AI codegen extension
outcome: Codeium/Windsurf reached $82M ARR and 350+ enterprise customers before Cognition acquired it in 2025.
outcomeDetail: Codeium raised a $150M Series C at a $1.25B valuation in 2024, rebranded around the Windsurf IDE, and reached $82M ARR with more than 350 enterprise customers. Cognition acquired Windsurf in July 2025.
note: The privacy concern was legitimate for a cloud code assistant, and Codeium responded with enterprise and on-prem options. The free tier did not make users the product in the way gigatexal feared.

author: perbu
cardQuote: I asked it to implement a -dry-run function. It failed twice. First time it just mangled the file. Second time it just made code that didn't do anything.
quote: I have this 300 line Go application which manages git tags for me. I asked it to implement a -dry-run function. It failed twice. First time it just mangled the file. Second time it just made code that didn't do anything. I asked it to rename a global variable. It broke the application and failed to understand scoping rules. Perhaps it is bad luck, or perhaps my Go code is weird, but I don't understand how y'all wanna trust this.
storyTitle: Aider: AI pair programming in your terminal
outcome: Aider grew to roughly 49,000 GitHub stars and remains one of the most widely used open-source terminal coding agents.
outcomeDetail: Aider became a standard terminal-based AI pair programmer, with its polyglot benchmark widely cited in model evaluations. It grew to roughly 49,000 GitHub stars and remains an active open-source project.
note: perbu's small Go refactor is a concrete example of the reliability gap that kept AI coding agents from replacing developers. Aider still became a widely used tool, but the failure mode he described remained familiar.

author: wokwokwok
cardQuote: If you see someone building a UI ... it means they're doing the easy work (part 1) because they don't know how to do the hard part (part 2).
quote: There are two parts to “writing a Devin”. 1) a pretty user interface, a backend service layer, all the normal things you’d need for a desktop app or saas. 2) a backend that can actually do work. I’m going to go out a limb here and say, building an MVP of the UI is a waste of your time. …because, unless you know how to build the backend (ie. part 2), you actually, have no idea what you need to build for part one . You can copy of the UI from the Devin videos. You can build your own langchain framework. You can fine tune an open model on GitHub issues. …but just like having building a gpt4 is harder than just “add more params”, building something that works like Devin appears to work requires a reasonably sharp “step up” in capability between what literally everyone has been doing with gpt4 until now, and being able to turn that into a useful framework for solving actual engineering tasks. So… don’t hold your breath. If you see someone building a UI (like this https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/tree/main/frontend , https://github.com/stitionai/devika/tree/main/ui ; just read the commit log, it’s basically just ui) it means they’re doing the easy work (part 1) because they don’t know how to do the hard part (part 2). …so, interesting, but this doesn’t smell like a really serious effort (at least yet). I guess you could argue that it’s important “setup infrastructure” stuff that any project starts with… but I’m just sceptical. I can draw pictures of a Devin too. A serious effort would be trying to replicate what Devin does not what it looks like .
outcome: OpenDevin became OpenHands, passed 60,000 GitHub stars, and raised an $18.8M Series A in 2025.
outcomeDetail: OpenDevin renamed itself OpenHands and grew into one of the most-starred open-source coding agents, with more than 60,000 GitHub stars. It raised an $18.8M Series A led by Madrona in November 2025 and launched a cloud agent platform for enterprises.
note: wokwokwok judged the project by its frontend commits and predicted it was avoiding the hard part. OpenHands built the agent runtime, attracted a large contributor base, and became a funded company.

quote: No mention of extensibility is a big red flag, and if it isn't open-source it presents the same risk as anyone adopting Atom originally ended up getting burned by.
storyTitle: Zed, the new code editor from Atom developers, has entered open beta
outcome: Zed open-sourced in 2024, raised a $32M Series B in 2025, and reported 150,000 active developers.
outcomeDetail: Zed open-sourced its editor in January 2024 and later added a WASM-based extension system. It raised a $32M Series B led by Sequoia in August 2025 and reported 150,000 active developers.
note: sjm's warning was fair at launch, but Zed addressed both concerns: it open-sourced the editor and built extensibility. It did not repeat Atom's shutdown.

quote: The project is a buzzword bingo roadmap (Rust! WASM! io_uring! Distributed databases!), a new CoC and license, and zero new code. No new code means I can’t take it seriously and I doubt they will ever deliver.
storyTitle: LibSQL is an open source, open contribution fork of SQLite
outcome: Turso delivered libSQL, rebuilt SQLite in Rust, and was acquired by Supabase in October 2026.
outcomeDetail: Turso shipped libSQL as an open-source SQLite fork and later rewrote SQLite in Rust, releasing a production alpha in 2025. Supabase acquired Turso in October 2026 to scale database infrastructure for AI agents.
note: Kwpolska saw a roadmap with no code and predicted non-delivery. Turso shipped the database, then became an acquisition target for one of the biggest developer-platform companies.

Haven't seen it since. > Parcel: The zero configuration build tool for JavaScript, CSS, HTML, TypeScript, React, images, SASS, SVG, Vue, libraries, Less, CoffeeScript, Node, Stylus, Pug, Electron, Elm, WebGL, extensions, GraphQL, MD As long as you do the bare minimum for each target.
storyTitle: Bun: Fast JavaScript runtime, transpiler, and NPM client written in Zig
outcome: Bun 1.0 shipped in September 2023, passed 7 million monthly downloads, and was acquired by Anthropic in December 2025.
outcomeDetail: Bun 1.0 shipped in September 2023 and became a popular all-in-one runtime, package manager, bundler, and test runner. Anthropic acquired Bun in December 2025, citing its role powering Claude Code and the Claude Agent SDK.
note: The Parcel/Rome comparison was meant to foreshadow a half-finished toolkit. Bun reached production stability, crossed 7 million monthly downloads, and became infrastructure for Anthropic's coding products.

author: halostatue
cardQuote: There's always a schema, and learning to manage it is a good thing. If you're not ready to manage and migrate, then you're not in production.
quote: Amy I the only person reading this who doesn’t think that the marketing line in the middle about not managing a schema is super scary? > Developers want the durability, stability, and scalability of a SQL database but do not want to be constrained by managing a schema. It has been our goal to give both, not compromising on the power of your datastore but making changes feel as easy as deploying code. Sorry. There’s always a schema, and learning to manage it is a _good_ thing. If you’re not ready to manage and migrate, then you’re not in production. You’re in something else.
outcome: PlanetScale raised a $50M Series C at general availability in 2021, with customers including GitHub, Slack, Square, and Affirm.
outcomeDetail: PlanetScale raised a $50M Series C led by Kleiner Perkins in November 2021, bringing total funding to $105M. Its schema-branching and non-blocking migration workflow became a reference point for developer-first MySQL, with customers including GitHub, Slack, Square, and Affirm.
note: halostatue read the marketing as an attempt to hide schema management. PlanetScale's point was that schema changes could be automated and branched like code, and that workflow found a real market.

quote: this seems like brilliant tech that will unfortunately not succeed due to the business model. Cost/billing, forced outgoing requests, forced signup, and most of all, additional security risks. I'm not using a terminal with all my SSH keys if it is calling out to the internet.
storyTitle: Show HN: Warp, a Rust-based terminal
outcome: Warp raised a $50M Series B in 2023 and reported more than 100,000 weekly developers at companies including Netflix and Cisco.
outcomeDetail: Warp raised a $50M Series B led by Sequoia in June 2023. By 2024 it reported more than 100,000 weekly developers at companies including Netflix, Cisco, and Atlassian, and it later added Linux and Windows support.
note: awill predicted the telemetry and signup requirements would sink Warp. The concerns were real, but Warp kept the product free for individuals, raised a large Series B, and reached six-figure weekly usage.

storyTitle: Qwik: No hydration, auto lazy-loading, edge-optimized, and fun
outcome: Qwik reached 1.0 in 2023 and moved to community governance in 2024, but resumability remained a niche alternative to mainstream React hydration.
outcomeDetail: Qwik reached 1.0 in May 2023 and spun out to community governance under the QwikDev organization in 2024. Resumability remains its signature feature, but adoption stayed far below React, Vue, and Svelte.
note: llamaLord's dismissal of hydration as a mainstream pain point aged reasonably well: Qwik made a real technical advance, but most teams never treated hydration as the buying criterion.

author: CharlesW
cardQuote: I don't understand why they're building a type system when TypeScript exists... taking the high-risk path of boiling the ocean
quote: > "Building a full-fledged type system such as TypeScript is a massive effort; that’s why we decided to take a different direction and start by building a subset of the type system that requires stricter typing." I don't understand why they're building a type system when TypeScript exists, just to name one of great projects they mention. Is there a manifesto somewhere that describes why this project is taking the high-risk path of boiling the ocean, instead of defining a set of best-in-class projects and improving integration over time? (The "Philosophy" page in the docs isn't helpful in this respect.)
outcome: Biome 2.0 shipped in June 2025 with type-aware linting, and Vercel standardized on Biome and sponsored the work.
outcomeDetail: Biome 2.0 shipped in June 2025 with type-aware lint rules, plugins, and multi-file analysis. Vercel standardized on Biome internally and sponsored the type-inference effort, and the project continued shipping regular releases.
note: CharlesW saw the type-inference roadmap as an attempt to rebuild TypeScript. Biome built only the type-aware linting subset it needed, shipped it in 2.0, and turned the scope risk into a differentiator.
